layers.title: Where published sites of any kind from 10,000–5000 BCE tend to be recorded
caveats: Held-out AUC 0.71 (folds 0.61 to 0.73) against 0.75 for a null that only knows survey effort. This layer does NOT beat the effort-only null. Read it as a map of where catalogues are dense.
The top-scoring 10% of documented area holds 17% of held-out presence cells (95% interval 14% to 20%); chance would be 10%.
Fitted without a whole macro-region and tested on it, AUC runs from 0.51 (Asia) to 0.59 (Africa and Near East). 0.5 is chance: the pattern is regional and does not carry over to other continents.

Only sites with a published date range count for this period. Most sites are undated, and most dated ones come from the Pleiades gazetteer of the Mediterranean and Near East, so this layer partly shows where that gazetteer reaches.
Shows where published sites of this kind tend to be recorded, relative to other cells that hold any published site. It is not a map of undiscovered sites and it cannot find one.
The published record follows where people have surveyed and what got catalogued. Comparing only against documented cells reduces that bias. It does not remove it.
Cells are 0.25 degrees, about 28 km at the equator. Far too coarse to point at a place.

Rivers are present-day drainage lines ranked by upstream area (HydroSHEDS), so they include dry desert channels. Coasts are present-day (ETOPO 2022). Climate is a model reconstruction (CHELSA-TraCE21k), not a measurement. None of it sees buried or drowned landscapes.
Grey cells are 'no basis': fewer than 10 documented cells lie within about 2.5 degrees, or a covariate is outside the range the model learned from. That is most of the world.
Straight east-west steps in the colours are a model artefact of using latitude, not a feature of the ground.
Labels come from Wikidata and Pleiades. OpenStreetMap sites are left out.
